source.title: Getting Past Your Breakup
source.attribution: A summary of Getting Past Your Breakup: How to Turn a Devastating Loss into the Best Thing That Ever Happened to You by Susan J. Elliott (2009). Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.
source.notes: Original summary written by Reborn; contains no text from the book. The book is in copyright.

cards.title: After a breakup, choose to heal rather than chase or pretend
cards.body:
Elliott describes three common ways people react when a relationship ends. Some try to win the ex back. Some act as if nothing happened and rush on. A third group stops, feels the loss and looks honestly at what happened.

She argues the third path is the hardest but the only one that leads to real recovery. Chasing keeps you stuck in someone else's choices, and pretending just buries the pain until it shows up later. Facing the loss turns a painful ending into a chance to grow.
cards.apply_it: Be honest: this week, have you mostly been chasing, pretending or healing? Write one small step toward healing.

quiz.question: Which response to a breakup does Elliott see as the path to real recovery?
options: Feeling the loss and looking honestly at what happened
Trying hard to win the ex back
Acting as if nothing happened
Starting a new relationship straight away
quiz.explanation: Elliott says facing the loss is the hardest path but the one that actually leads to healing.

cards.title: Go 'no contact' to give yourself room to heal
cards.body:
The best-known idea in Elliott's book is no contact: after the relationship ends, stop calling, texting, visiting and meeting your ex. Every conversation reopens the wound and feeds hope that things might change, so the healing clock keeps resetting.

Elliott presents no contact as something you do for yourself, not a punishment or a tactic to make the ex miss you. Distance lets your feelings settle and gives you space to focus on your own life instead of on what the other person is doing or thinking.
cards.apply_it: Decide today what no contact will mean for you, and write it down so you can hold to it on hard days.

quiz.question: Why does Elliott recommend no contact after a breakup?
options: It makes the ex miss you and come back
It punishes the ex for leaving
It proves you have already moved on
It gives you space to heal instead of reopening the wound
quiz.explanation: No contact is for your own healing, not a strategy to influence the ex.

cards.title: No contact includes not checking their social media
cards.body:
Elliott points out that people often stop phoning an ex but keep watching them online: scrolling their photos, checking who they follow, reading old messages. It feels harmless, but each look stirs up longing, jealousy or fresh questions, and you end up living in their world instead of yours.

She treats this kind of monitoring as part of contact. Muting, unfollowing or blocking isn't childish or dramatic; it is a practical boundary that protects your attention while you heal.
cards.apply_it: Mute or unfollow your ex on one app today, and remove the shortcut that tempts you to check.

quiz.question: How does Elliott view checking an ex's social media?
options: As a healthy way to get closure
As a form of contact that keeps you stuck
As harmless if you don't message them
As the best way to know when to reach out
quiz.explanation: Watching an ex online keeps the wound open, so she counts it as contact.

cards.title: If you must stay in touch, keep contact limited and businesslike
cards.body:
Elliott recognises that full no contact isn't always possible. You may share children, work in the same place or have money or property to sort out. In those cases she suggests limited contact: keep exchanges brief, polite and about the practical matter only.

That means no long late-night talks, no reopening old arguments and no digging into their new life. Writing rather than calling, or agreeing set times for handovers, can help. The aim is to cooperate where you must while still protecting your heart.
cards.apply_it: If you share practical matters with an ex, draft a short, polite template message you can reuse so you stay on task.

quiz.question: What does Elliott suggest when you can't fully cut contact, for example when you share children?
options: Long talks to understand each other better
Brief, polite contact about practical matters only
Avoiding them even when the children need it
Staying friends as if nothing changed
quiz.explanation: Limited contact lets you cooperate on practical things while protecting your healing.

cards.title: Don't wait for your ex to give you closure
cards.body:
Many people hold on, hoping for one more conversation that will finally explain why it ended. Elliott warns that this closure talk rarely delivers. The ex may not know the answer, may not tell you honestly, or may say something that hurts more.

In her view, closure is something you build yourself: by grieving, reflecting on the relationship and accepting that it is over even without a satisfying explanation. Taking that job back from your ex is part of reclaiming your life.
cards.apply_it: Write down the question you most want your ex to answer. Then write your own best, honest answer to it.

quiz.question: According to Elliott, where does closure usually come from?
options: A final honest talk with your ex
Seeing your ex unhappy
Finding out who they are dating now
Your own grieving, reflection and acceptance
quiz.explanation: She argues you create closure yourself instead of waiting for the ex to provide it.

cards.title: Notice the excuses you invent to reach out
cards.body:
Elliott observes how creative the mind gets after a breakup: returning a book, wishing them happy birthday, checking they are okay, asking about a shared friend. These reasons feel innocent, but often they are a way to get a reaction or reopen the door.

She suggests seeing them for what they are. Practical things can be handled once, in a planned way, or through a friend. When the urge comes, pause and ask what you are really hoping will happen, then do something kind for yourself instead.
cards.apply_it: Next time you want to contact your ex, write the reason down and ask: what am I really hoping for?

quiz.question: What does Elliott say about 'innocent' reasons to contact an ex?
options: They are often excuses to get a reaction or reopen the door
They are always fine if you are polite
They help both people heal faster
They should be acted on quickly before they fade
quiz.explanation: She encourages you to spot these excuses and handle genuine practical matters in a planned way.

cards.title: A breakup is a real loss, and it needs to be grieved
cards.body:
Elliott treats the end of a relationship as a genuine loss that deserves grieving, not something to brush off. You lose a person, but also routines, plans, a sense of security and the future you pictured.

She warns that putting on a brave face does not make the pain disappear; it just goes underground. Letting yourself cry, talk and feel the sadness may seem like going backwards, yet it is how the loss is digested so you can genuinely move on.
cards.apply_it: List three things besides the person that you lost when the relationship ended. Allow yourself to feel each one.

quiz.question: Why does Elliott say hiding your pain behind strength doesn't work?
options: Strength is a sign you never loved them
People will judge you for being strong
The pain doesn't go away; it just goes underground
Grief only lasts a few days anyway
quiz.explanation: Unfelt grief stays with you; feeling it is how you work through it.

cards.title: Expect your feelings to swing, and let them
cards.body:
Grief after a breakup does not move neatly from one stage to the next, Elliott explains. You may feel numb one day, furious the next, then sad, then oddly hopeful, and then back again. Shock, anger, confusion and longing are all part of it.

She encourages accepting these swings instead of fighting them or judging yourself for being 'still upset'. A bad day after a good week isn't failure. Over time the waves usually come less often and hurt less.
cards.apply_it: When a strong feeling arrives today, name it out loud or on paper without judging it: 'This is anger,' 'This is sadness.'

quiz.question: How does Elliott describe the grief that follows a breakup?
options: A neat sequence of stages, one after another
A single feeling of sadness
Unpredictable swings between different feelings
Something that should be over in a week
quiz.explanation: Grief moves back and forth; accepting that is part of healing.

cards.title: A breakup can stir up older, unhealed losses
cards.body:
Elliott notes that the pain of a breakup sometimes feels bigger than the relationship itself. That can be because it touches older losses that were never fully grieved: a parent's absence, an earlier rejection, a death or a disappointing childhood.

She argues that unresolved grief builds up and can make us fearful and shape how we love. Using this breakup as a chance to look at, and grieve, those older hurts can free you from carrying them into the next relationship.
cards.apply_it: Ask yourself: does this pain remind me of an older loss? Write a few lines about that earlier experience.

quiz.question: Why might a breakup hurt more than the relationship alone seems to explain?
options: It can stir up older losses that were never grieved
Because the relationship was perfect
Because pain always grows over time
Because you are weaker than other people
quiz.explanation: Elliott says unresolved past grief can add to the weight of a new loss.

cards.title: Plan ahead for anniversaries, birthdays and holidays
cards.body:
Certain days hit harder: the anniversary of meeting, their birthday, festive seasons, the date you broke up. Elliott advises expecting this rather than being ambushed by it.

Planning helps. Arrange to spend the day with friends or family, book something you enjoy, or give yourself permission for a quiet, gentle day. Knowing a difficult date is coming, and having a plan, makes it something you get through rather than something that knocks you flat.
cards.apply_it: Check your calendar for the next date likely to be hard, and plan one supportive thing for that day now.

quiz.question: What does Elliott suggest about painful dates such as anniversaries?
options: Ignore them and hope they pass
Contact your ex on those days
Avoid all people on those days
Expect them and plan supportive things to do
quiz.explanation: Anticipating hard dates and making a plan softens their impact.

cards.title: Keep a journal to work through the breakup
cards.body:
Journaling is one of Elliott's core tools. Writing regularly, even briefly, gives your thoughts somewhere to go instead of looping in your head at night. It helps you name what you feel, notice what triggers you and see patterns you might miss.

A journal also becomes a record of progress. Weeks later you can read back and see how far you have come, which is encouraging on days when it feels as though nothing has changed.
cards.apply_it: Tonight, write for ten minutes: what you felt today, what triggered it and one thing you did that helped.

quiz.question: Besides releasing feelings, what extra benefit of journaling does Elliott highlight?
options: It replaces the need for any other support
It becomes a record that shows your progress over time
It helps you plan how to win your ex back
It proves who was to blame
quiz.explanation: Reading back over a journal shows you how far you have come.

cards.title: Write letters to your ex that you never send
cards.body:
Elliott suggests writing letters to your ex as a way to say everything left unsaid: the anger, the sadness, the questions, the thank-yous. The key is that the letters are for you. Sending them usually reopens contact and invites a reply you can't control.

Putting it all on paper lets the feelings out without the risk. Some people keep the letters, others tear them up or burn them as a small ritual of release.
cards.apply_it: Write a letter to your ex saying everything you wish you could say. Do not send it; decide whether to keep it or let it go.

quiz.question: What is the point of the letters Elliott suggests writing to an ex?
options: To persuade the ex to come back
To express what's unsaid, for your own healing, without sending them
To make the ex feel guilty
To get the last word in the argument
quiz.explanation: The letters are a private release; sending them would reopen contact.

cards.title: Take an honest inventory of the relationship
cards.body:
After a breakup it's easy to remember only the best moments. Elliott recommends listing the relationship's positives and negatives in writing, including how your ex behaved and how you felt.

Seeing the full picture on paper helps counter the rose-tinted version your mind replays. It can show you what really wasn't working, what you put up with and which needs went unmet. This isn't about building a case against the other person; it is about seeing clearly so you can learn.
cards.apply_it: Draw two columns: what was good and what wasn't working. Fill in at least five lines on each side.

quiz.question: Why does Elliott suggest listing both the good and bad sides of the relationship?
options: To prove the ex was a bad person
To decide whether to get back together
To share the list with friends
To see it clearly instead of only remembering the best moments
quiz.explanation: A written inventory balances the idealised memories with reality.

cards.title: Look at your own part without beating yourself up
cards.body:
Elliott encourages looking honestly at your own role in the relationship as well as your ex's. Did you ignore warning signs, give up things that mattered to you, or avoid hard conversations?

The point is understanding, not blame. Relationships end for many reasons, and taking responsibility for your part is different from deciding everything was your fault. Seeing your own patterns is actually empowering: it is the part you can change.
cards.apply_it: Write one thing you would do differently next time, then one kind sentence to yourself about why you didn't do it before.

quiz.question: What is the goal of examining your own part in the relationship?
options: Understanding what you can change, without self-blame
Proving that everything was your fault
Finding reasons to apologise to your ex
Deciding you should never date again
quiz.explanation: Owning your part is about learning, not punishing yourself.

cards.title: Keep a gratitude list to steady your outlook
cards.body:
When you are hurting, your attention narrows to what you have lost. Elliott suggests deliberately noting what is still good: friends who called, a meal you enjoyed, a skill you have, a moment of peace.

A gratitude list doesn't deny the pain or rush you to feel fine. It simply widens the view so the breakup isn't the only thing you see. Over time, the habit can lift your mood and remind you that your life is bigger than this loss.
cards.apply_it: Before bed tonight, write three things, however small, that you are grateful for today.

quiz.question: What does a gratitude list do, according to Elliott's approach?
options: Forces you to stop feeling sad
Replaces the need to grieve
Widens your view beyond the loss without denying the pain
Shows your ex that you are fine
quiz.explanation: It balances your outlook while still allowing grief.

cards.title: Replace harsh self-talk with kinder words
cards.body:
A breakup often sets off a cruel inner voice: you weren't enough, you'll always be alone, it's all your fault. Elliott gives a lot of weight to changing this self-talk, including the use of affirmations, short positive statements you repeat until they start to feel true.

The point isn't pretending everything is fine. It is noticing when you speak to yourself in a way you would never speak to a friend, and choosing words that are more accurate and supportive. Rebuilding self-esteem starts with the way you talk to yourself every day.
cards.apply_it: Write one harsh thing you've been telling yourself, then rewrite it the way a loyal friend would say it.

quiz.question: What does Elliott suggest doing about the harsh inner voice after a breakup?
options: Agree with it so you learn your lesson
Ignore all thoughts about yourself
Notice it and replace it with kinder, more accurate words
Ask your ex whether it is true
quiz.explanation: Changing self-talk, including through affirmations, helps rebuild self-esteem.

cards.title: Look after your body while your heart heals
cards.body:
Grief is exhausting, and Elliott stresses basic physical care during a breakup: eat regular meals, move your body, and protect your sleep as best you can. Exercise, a walk outside or simple stretching can release tension and lift your mood.

These things can feel trivial next to heartbreak, but they give you the energy to cope. When the basics slip, everything feels heavier. If you are struggling to sleep or eat for a long time, it is worth speaking to a doctor.
cards.apply_it: Pick one basic to protect this week: a regular bedtime, one proper meal a day, or a 20-minute walk.

quiz.question: Why does Elliott emphasise eating, sleep and exercise after a breakup?
options: Looking after your body gives you energy to cope with grief
They distract you so you never think about the ex
They help you look good for your ex
They replace the need to grieve
quiz.explanation: Basic physical care supports you through an exhausting emotional time.

cards.title: Don't numb the pain with drink or a quick rebound
cards.body:
Elliott warns against the shortcuts people reach for to avoid feeling the loss: drinking more, overworking, endless partying or jumping straight into a new relationship. They may bring short relief, but they delay grieving and can add new problems.

A rebound in particular can mean carrying unhealed hurt into the next relationship. Facing the feelings is slower and harder, but it is what actually lets you heal. If you find you are relying on alcohol or other substances to get through, reach out for professional help.
cards.apply_it: Notice what you reach for when the pain hits. Choose one healthier option to try next time.

quiz.question: Why does Elliott caution against a quick rebound relationship?
options: Because you should never date again
Because rebounds always make the ex jealous
Because it is better to rely on alcohol
It can delay grieving and carry old hurt into the new relationship
quiz.explanation: Numbing shortcuts postpone the healing work rather than replace it.

cards.title: Give your days structure while grief scrambles your mind
cards.body:
Grief can make you forgetful and scattered. You lose your keys, forget appointments and struggle to concentrate. Elliott recommends leaning on simple structure: a daily schedule, to-do lists and reminders.

She also suggests building in a little downtime each day, such as a warm bath, a walk or a favourite pastime, and ending the day by reflecting on something you did well. Structure doesn't fix the pain, but it keeps life moving and gives you small wins on hard days.
cards.apply_it: Write tomorrow's plan tonight: three tasks, one pleasant activity and a time to stop and rest.

quiz.question: How does Elliott suggest coping with the forgetfulness and disorganisation grief can bring?
options: Stay in bed until the feeling passes
Use schedules, lists and small daily routines
Ask your ex to help you stay organised
Take on as much extra work as possible
quiz.explanation: Simple structure keeps daily life on track while you grieve.

cards.title: Revive old interests and try new ones
cards.body:
Elliott encourages using the time after a breakup to put your attention back on your own life. Pick up hobbies you dropped during the relationship, try something you've always wanted to do, join a class, club, faith group or volunteer team, and reconnect with friends.

New activities ease stress and help you discover parts of yourself that may have been sidelined. She also advises balance: time with people, and some time alone to rest and reflect.
cards.apply_it: Name one interest you let go of during the relationship and take one small step to restart it this week.

quiz.question: What does Elliott suggest about hobbies and social life after a breakup?
options: Stay home until you feel completely better
Revive old interests, try new ones and balance company with time alone
Only do activities your ex enjoyed
Fill every hour so you never have time to think
quiz.explanation: Rebuilding your own interests helps you rediscover yourself.

cards.title: Get support: friends, groups or a counsellor
cards.body:
You don't have to get through a breakup alone. Elliott recommends leaning on people who care about you, and also considers professional help: a therapist or counsellor, or a support group of people going through something similar.

Others who understand can normalise what you are feeling and offer perspective you can't see from inside the pain. If your sadness becomes overwhelming, lasts a long time, or you have thoughts of harming yourself, contact a doctor or a crisis line straight away.
cards.apply_it: Message one person you trust today and tell them honestly how you're doing.

quiz.question: Which kinds of support does Elliott suggest after a breakup?
options: Only your ex, because they understand best
None, because healing should be done alone
Only online strangers
Friends and family, therapists or counsellors, and support groups
quiz.explanation: She encourages a mix of personal and professional support.

cards.title: Mark the ending with a personal ritual
cards.body:
Weddings and anniversaries have ceremonies, but endings usually don't. Elliott suggests creating your own ritual to mark that the relationship is over: burning or burying an unsent letter, planting something, taking a meaningful walk, or saying a few words with a trusted friend present.

A ritual gives a clear moment of release. It turns a vague, drawn-out ending into something you consciously chose to complete, which can make letting go feel more real.
cards.apply_it: Design a simple ritual to mark the end of the relationship, and choose a day to do it.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of the rituals Elliott suggests?
options: To give a clear moment that marks the end and helps you let go
To win the ex back
To celebrate that the ex is suffering
To avoid feeling anything
quiz.explanation: A ritual creates a conscious moment of release.

cards.title: Clear the reminders out of your daily space
cards.body:
Photos on the wall, gifts on the shelf, their clothes in the cupboard, old messages on your phone: reminders can keep pulling you back into the relationship many times a day. Elliott suggests clearing your space of them.

You don't have to destroy everything. You might box up items and store them somewhere out of sight, or give them to a friend to keep for now. Shared children's photos and important documents stay. The aim is a home that supports your new life rather than the old one.
cards.apply_it: Choose one area of your home or phone and box up or archive the reminders there this week.

quiz.question: What does Elliott suggest doing with reminders of the relationship?
options: Keep them visible so you remember the good times
Send them all back to the ex with a long letter
Clear them from your daily space, for example by storing them out of sight
Look at them each day to toughen yourself up
quiz.explanation: Reducing reminders stops them reopening the wound every day.

cards.title: Forgive for your own peace, not to excuse what happened
cards.body:
Elliott sees forgiveness, of your ex and of yourself, as part of letting go. Forgiveness here means releasing the grip that resentment has on you. It doesn't mean saying the hurt was acceptable, and it doesn't require getting back together or even staying in touch.

It often comes slowly and after real grieving, not as a quick decision. If the relationship involved abuse, your safety comes first; you owe no contact or reconciliation, and a domestic abuse helpline can support you.
cards.apply_it: Write: 'I am ready to stop carrying ___.' Notice how it feels, even if you are not fully ready yet.

quiz.question: What does forgiveness mean in Elliott's approach?
options: Agreeing to get back together
Pretending the hurt never happened
Releasing resentment's hold on you, not excusing the hurt
Telling the ex they did nothing wrong
quiz.explanation: Forgiveness is for your peace; it doesn't excuse harm or require contact.

cards.title: Reassure children that both parents still love them
cards.body:
When there are children, Elliott devotes a chapter to helping them through the breakup. A central message is reassurance: the separation is not their fault, and both parents will keep loving them.

She advises answering their questions patiently and honestly but in simple, age-appropriate terms, without adult details about who did what. Children may ask the same questions many times; calm, consistent answers help them feel secure.
cards.apply_it: Prepare a short, simple sentence you can use when your child asks why you separated, free of blame or adult details.

quiz.question: What does Elliott say children most need to hear after their parents separate?
options: It is not their fault and both parents still love them
Exactly which parent caused the breakup
That nothing at all will change
That they should choose a parent to live with
quiz.explanation: Reassurance about love and blame helps children feel secure.

cards.title: Keep children out of the middle of adult conflict
cards.body:
Elliott urges separated parents not to use children as messengers, spies or confidants, and not to criticise the other parent in front of them. Children usually love both parents, and being pulled into the conflict forces them into an impossible position.

Keeping routines steady and staying organised also helps them cope. Adult feelings about the breakup belong with adult friends, a counsellor or a support group, not with the children.
cards.apply_it: If you need to vent about your ex, choose an adult to call instead, and keep messages about logistics between the parents.

quiz.question: According to Elliott, how should parents handle their conflict around the children?
options: Explain every detail so children understand
Let children decide who was right
Ask children to report on the other parent's life
Keep children out of it: no messengers, no criticism of the other parent
quiz.explanation: Children shouldn't carry adult conflict; adults should take their feelings elsewhere.

cards.title: Find where you struggle to say no
cards.body:
Elliott argues that a lot of relationship pain comes from weak boundaries: going along with things you didn't want, keeping quiet to avoid conflict, or letting your needs come last. She suggests reviewing past relationships to find moments when you couldn't say no or disagree.

Then look at your current relationships, with family, friends and at work, for places where a clearer limit would help. Boundaries protect your wellbeing and help others know how to treat you. If someone repeatedly ignores your limits or tries to control you, that is a warning sign worth taking seriously.
cards.apply_it: Recall one time you said yes when you meant no. What would you say if it happened today?

quiz.question: Why does Elliott ask readers to look back at times they couldn't say no?
options: To blame others for your problems
To spot weak boundaries so you can set clearer limits now
To prove you were always too nice
To find reasons to contact your ex
quiz.explanation: Spotting past boundary problems helps you protect yourself going forward.

cards.title: Spot your patterns and decide your standards
cards.body:
Looking across your past relationships, and your life more widely, Elliott suggests asking what keeps repeating. Do you choose partners who are unavailable? Do you lose yourself, or ignore early red flags?

Once you see a pattern, you can decide what you value and what you will and won't accept in future. Writing these standards down gives you something firm to check against when a new person comes along, so you don't simply repeat an old cycle.
cards.apply_it: Write three things you will expect in your next relationship and two things you will no longer accept.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of reviewing patterns across past relationships?
options: To prove all partners are the same
To see what repeats and set clear standards for the future
To decide never to trust anyone
To find a partner exactly like your ex
quiz.explanation: Seeing patterns lets you set standards and break unhealthy cycles.

cards.title: Date again when you're whole, not when you're lonely
cards.body:
Elliott's advice on dating is about readiness rather than a fixed timetable. You are ready when you can enjoy your life on your own and don't need someone else to make you happy or to fill the gap the ex left.

She argues that dating from neediness makes it easier to overlook red flags and settle for someone who isn't good for you. Feeling steady and independent makes it more likely you will choose a partner who is genuinely right.
cards.apply_it: Ask yourself honestly: would I be fine if I stayed single for the next year? Note what your answer tells you.

quiz.question: When does Elliott suggest you are ready to date again?
options: As soon as possible, to forget the ex
Exactly six months after the breakup
When your ex starts dating
When you can enjoy life without needing a partner to make you happy
quiz.explanation: Readiness is about feeling whole on your own, not a calendar date.

cards.title: When love comes again, don't give up your own life
cards.body:
Elliott warns against a common trap: meeting someone new and gradually dropping your friends, interests and goals to fit around them. That loss of self can recreate the conditions of the last painful relationship.

A healthy new relationship adds to your life rather than replacing it. Keep the hobbies, friendships and plans you rebuilt after the breakup. Two people with full lives of their own make a stronger, more balanced partnership.
cards.apply_it: List the activities and friendships you rebuilt after your breakup, and promise yourself you'll keep them in a new relationship.

quiz.question: What does Elliott advise when you start a new relationship?
options: Keep your own friends, interests and goals
Give up your hobbies to show commitment
Spend every free moment with the new partner
Cut contact with friends who knew your ex
quiz.explanation: A healthy relationship adds to your life instead of replacing it.
